input:
You are a critic of research topics. Below are topic candidates for a study that an AI agent will carry out autonomously. Point out the weaknesses of each candidate.

The main readers of this study are researchers working on the social problem addressed and practitioners in government, business, communities and other settings (both humans and AIs). A good topic is one where readers' understanding or judgment changes between before and after reading the results. Each study takes 12 hours and is carried out within the range of local compute, public data and a small amount of AI API use.

For each candidate, look for weaknesses from the following points of view.
1. Effect on readers: Which understanding or judgment, concretely, would researchers and practitioners who read the results change? If they would not change any, say so.
2. Generality: Do the results hold beyond a particular tool, library version or dataset? Will they not become outdated in a few months?
3. Realism: Is there a risk that the effect appears only under artificial conditions or with inputs that are rare in reality? Are realistic inputs excluded from the targets?
4. Novelty: Is there close prior work or a known result (including what is already known from official statistics, reports or white papers)? Does it amount to no more than re-confirming a known concern with numbers?
5. Unpredictability: Could the result be largely predicted without experiments?
6. Size of the question: Has it become a solid but small question?

Before naming close prior work, confirm it by web search. Also look for literature and preprints from 2025 onward. Include the standard methods and classic studies of the field. Also check whether the same problem has been studied under a different name in other fields.

For each candidate, write in the following format.
- The most serious weakness (with the number of the point of view above)
- Prior work that seems close (authors, title, year, URL; write "unconfirmed" for any you could not confirm by web search)
- A scenario in which the value would be small even if it succeeds
- A direction that broadens the question or brings it closer to reality (at most one, within the scope of that candidate; do not propose new topics)

Do not rank the candidates. You have not been told which candidate is planned to be adopted.

Candidate list:
Q01
Question: When heat-response capacity is shared across regions, can medium-range joint weather forecasts identify days on which usual mutual-aid partners are simultaneously unavailable, and does forecast-aware reservation improve on fixed geographic pooling?
Method outline: Replay shared-capacity reservation decisions on archived coherent forecast trajectories and verifying temperature events. Compare joint forecasts, matched marginal forecasts with independent or historical dependence, fixed geographic pools, and climatology at multiple reservation costs and leads. Temperature exceedance is an explicit proxy for response demand. Access to recent-model surface ensemble hindcasts is uncertain; available NeuralGCM output has upper-air fields only, so do not silently substitute it.
Closest work and difference: Golkar et al., Forecast lead time and the timing of crew deployment for weather-driven power outages using AI weather models (2026), https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20918, studies ranked staging and externally specified crew availability; the proposed contrast predicts joint donor unavailability. Schefzik et al., Uncertainty Quantification in Complex Simulation Models Using Ensemble Copula Coupling (2013), https://arxiv.org/abs/1302.7149, establishes dependence-preserving postprocessing; the proposed outcome is capacity-sharing decisions, not a new copula method. Price et al., Probabilistic weather forecasting with machine learning (2025), https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-08252-9, already evaluates joint forecasts and wind-power aggregation.

Q02
Question: For low-wind electricity episodes, can a warning rule that accounts for forecast recovery time reduce premature reserve release compared with warnings based only on daily low-wind probabilities?
Method outline: Use archived ensemble trajectories and verifying wind/power proxies to compare recovery-aware and daily-marginal release decisions at matched reserve-days or stated reserve cost, with historical-run and coherent-postprocessing comparators. Turbine-height/near-surface data matching is required; an available upper-air-only archive is insufficient without a defensible mapping.
Closest work and difference: Schefzik et al., Uncertainty Quantification in Complex Simulation Models Using Ensemble Copula Coupling (2013), https://arxiv.org/abs/1302.7149, provides the established temporal-dependence machinery. Laugesen et al., Flexible forecast value metric suitable for a wide range of decisions: application using probabilistic subseasonal streamflow forecasts (2023), https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-27-873-2023, studies utility versus threshold decisions; the proposed specific contrast is reserve release during wind recovery. Patlakas et al., Low wind speed events: persistence and frequency (2017), https://doi.org/10.1002/we.2078, characterizes duration/frequency rather than forecast-conditioned release.

Q03
Question: Can annual satellite representations support claims of ecological recovery after wildfire when movement toward a pre-fire state is judged against matched stable vegetation rather than against the fire-year embedding alone?
Method outline: Compare annual embedding trajectories from TESSERA and AlphaEarth on public fire severity maps and matched stable land-cover controls, with conventional spectral-index recovery measures. Separate disturbance disappearance from return to pre-fire similarity and from biological recovery, which is not directly measured.
Closest work and difference: Knezevic et al., Annual Earth-observation embeddings encode wildfire disturbance and support simplified burned area mapping (2026), https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.25731, already compares two embedding families, pre/event/post-fire separability and transfer. Earth embeddings are decomposable records of the land surface (2026), https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32617, already examines controls, disturbance timing and persistence/recovery differences, leaving very little clear difference for the proposed question. Kennedy et al., Detecting trends in forest disturbance and recovery using yearly Landsat time series: 1. LandTrendr—Temporal segmentation algorithms (2010), https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rse.2010.07.008, is an established recovery comparator.

Q04
Question: Can crop-diversity change be estimated without annual relabeling when crop rotations alter the performance of a map trained in one reference year, and does a limited-label area adjustment preserve the direction of change?
Method outline: On public annual embedding samples and public crop-reference rasters, train a classifier in a reference year and freeze it across later years. Compare two representation families, conventional/static baselines where feasible, annually refreshed classifiers, source-year confusion adjustment, and probability-sampled limited target-year corrections under an explicit label budget. Evaluate errors in landscape crop proportions, Shannon diversity/effective crop number and their change, with spatially separated training/test units and paired uncertainty. Public classified crop maps are imperfect references; they are not field ground truth. Pilot embedding and matched crop-label access succeeded.
Closest work and difference: Lisaius et al., Embedding-based Crop Type Classification in the Groundnut Basin of Senegal (2026), https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.16900, measures plausibility and temporal classification transfer; the proposed contrast directly evaluates aggregate diversity-change error and budgeted corrections, not cross-year accuracy alone. Olofsson et al., Good practices for estimating area and assessing accuracy of land change (2014), https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rse.2014.02.015, establishes design-based area adjustment, which is a comparator rather than a proposed new estimator. Feng et al., TESSERA: Temporal Embeddings of Surface Spectra for Earth Representation and Analysis (2025/2026), https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.20380, benchmarks label-efficient crop classification; the proposed estimand is the direction and magnitude of monitoring change without full annual relabeling.

Q05
Question: For intermittent food/supply procurement, do probabilistic forecasts that are well calibrated for each future day give reliable total-demand reserves over a delivery interval, and can dependence-only correction improve service risk without altering daily distributions?
Method outline: Compare local public pretrained forecast trajectories, direct lead-time forecasts, Markov intermittent-demand bootstrap and empirical alternatives on public demand data. Reorder sample paths while holding daily marginals fixed; test summed-demand calibration and shortage/holding costs across lead times. Use a genuinely unseen demand source if possible; pilot car-parts data overlap pretraining and replace missing values by zero, so they are feasibility-only and do not represent food banks.
Closest work and difference: Willemain et al., A new approach to forecasting intermittent demand for service parts inventories (2004), https://doi.org/10.1016/S0169-2070(03)00013-X, already evaluates dependence-aware lead-time distributions with a Markov bootstrap; the proposed limited difference is immediate pretrained trajectories and matched-marginal repair. Ansari et al., Chronos: Learning the Language of Time Series (2024), https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07815, provides autoregressive paths but mostly marginal WQL/point evaluation. Kim and Song, When Time-Series Foundation Models Work for Quick-Commerce Demand Forecasting (2026), https://doi.org/10.13106/jidb.2026.vol17.no3.89, compares models across demand patterns and operational forecast bias; the proposed contrast is joint lead-time distributions and controlled dependence intervention.
